name: Punan Merap
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog puna1274 lists only classification comments (Sellato 2007; Smith 2017 dialect note); no phonological description found

new_statements.quote: [p.62-63] Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə. [p.68] Justifying the above vowel inventory is dependent on one's analysis of stress. Merap is a stress-final language, where the final syllable is always stressed. In every vowel phoneme presented above, stress falls on the initial segment. Thus, a is stressed as [ˈa], əw is stressed [ˈəw], ĩə̯ is stressed [ˈĩə̯], and ayə̯ is stressed [ˈayə̯].
new_statements.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The languages of Borneo: a comprehensive classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.2.2, pp. 62-63 (pp. 92-93); sec. 2.2.2.2 'More on Merap', p. 68 (p. 98); secondary stress sec. 2.2.2.2.3, p. 72 (p. 102)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (+; open, downloaded from the Internet Archive of ling.hawaii..). All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators, confirmed both in the (lines 3074-3079, 3283-3290, 3417-3420) and by extracted text on PDF pages 92, 98, 102 (printed pp. 62-63, 68, 72): (1) sec. 2.2.2 'Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə.'; (2) sec. 2.2.2.2 'More on Merap': 'Justifying the above…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Merap word stress is fixed on the final syllable and is phonetically strong; complex nuclei (diphthongs/triphthongs such as ayə̯, awə̯) count as a single final-syllable nucleus stressed on their first element, so apparent 'penultimate' stress in forms like [ˈayə̯] is final stress on a triphthong.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.72: 'words with CVCCVC structures receive a secondary stress in Merap; ˌCVCˈCVC' (secondary stress on a closed pre-final syllable; offered as a diagnostic for medial clusters).
new_statements.exceptions: None to finality; genuine vowel sequences exist (kiawə̯ 'Myna bird' [kiˈawə̯]) but are still final-stressed. Note a contradicting non-specialist claim: Radjaban, Humanika & Arafah 2025 (JLTR 16(3):960-961) assert meaning-distinguishing 'initial vs final stress' pairs in Merap, but their pairs differ in final -h vs glottal stop and the analysis is not credible against Smith's fieldwork description. Smith contrasts Merap (strong final) with its sister Ngorek/Murik (weak penultimate).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms from the author's own fieldwork at Langap (Malinau river); stress analysis is used to justify the 26-vowel inventory. Smith also places Merap in a central-Bornean area of strong word-final stress (Segai-Modang, Hliboi Bidayuh etc.).
new_statements.identity_note: puna1274 'Punan Merap' [puc] is a RETIRED Glottolog bookkeeping code. Glottolog 5.3: the label conflates (a) 'Punan Merap', former hunter-gatherers allied with the Merap who speak Punan Tubu [puj] = puna1266 (Sellato 2007; checked separately under, no accessible stress statement found there), and (b) the Merap (Mbraa/Mpraa) of Langap on the Malinau river, a Kayanic language = Glottolog mera1243, dialect-level under Murik (Malaysia) muri1259 (Smith 2017: sister of Ngorek in a Murik-Merap subgroup). Ethnologue 16's puc location ('east of Longkemuat', 200 speakers, Wurm & Hattori 1981) and Wikipedia both point to referent (b). The quoted statement describes referent (b), Merap of Langap. Any catalog entry should be keyed to mera1243 (or muri1259 with a Merap dialect note), not to the retired code puna1274; note that Smith describes the sister dialect Ngorek/Murik (Long Semiang, Sarawak) as having WEAK PENULTIMATE stress, so muri1259 is not uniform for stress and Merap must be kept distinct from Ngorek.

sources.citation: Radjaban, R. Yohanes; Humanika, Eko Setyo; Arafah, Burhanuddin. 2025. A holistic study of Merap language mapping in relation to the term Punan-Merap. Journal of Language Teaching and Research 16(3): 957-965. DOI 10.17507/jltr.1603.26.
sources.note: pp.960-961 claim stress/'tone' is meaning-distinguishing, with 'initial stress' vs 'final stress' pairs (Table 2: 'tuih 'white' ~ tui' 'banana', 'bau 'hair' ~ bau' 'bamboo shoot', etc.); the pairs visibly differ in final -h vs glottal stop, so this reads as a misanalysis of laryngeal codas; contradicts Smith 2017. Useful for identity: argues 'Punan-Merap' names Punan living alongside the Merap, not a language, and that Merap is Kayan-group.
